title: Scammers know the best time to text you
summary: Malwarebytes data reveals scam texts peak around noon ET with 874% higher volume than overnight, and Fridays bring roughly 50% more messages.
story: Clicking links in a fake party invitation email can install malware that gives criminals remote access to your computer and personal information, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

If your phone seems to light up with suspicious texts right when your day gets busy, you may not be imagining it. New research from cybersecurity company Malwarebytes suggests scammers have gotten much more strategic about when they contact you and where they do it.

The company analyzed global threat data collected between April 15 and July 14, 2026. Researchers tracked more than 20 scam categories. They found that criminals often choose the platform that gives a particular scam the best chance of working.

Then there is the timing. For Americans, scam text volume peaked around 12 p.m. ET. That was about 874% higher than at 1 a.m. ET, the quietest hour Malwarebytes observed. Scam text volume also climbed as the week went on. It reached its highest point on Friday, when people received roughly 50% more fraudulent texts than at the beginning of the week.

That tells me scammers are paying attention to more than what they send you. They are also watching when you may be most likely to see it. And the timing is only part of the strategy, because the type of scam often determines exactly where they try to reach you.
THE SCAM TEXT TEST: SPOT DANGER BEFORE YOU TAP
Scam texts can catch you while you are busy, distracted and more likely to react before checking the message. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your healthcare. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed.
Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
Scammers are choosing the best place to reach you

Different scams tend to favor different platforms. Malwarebytes found that job scams commonly arrive through email. Romance scams favor social media, where conversations with new people feel more natural. Meanwhile, tech support scams frequently start with a phone call. That makes sense when you think about how each scam works.

A fake recruiter can blend into a busy inbox. Someone starting a conversation on social media may seem harmless. A caller claiming your computer has a serious problem can immediately put you under pressure.
The channel becomes part of the trick. We've seen that with changing tech support scams. They can now begin with fake invoices, bogus security alerts or convincing support pages.
The web remains scammers' favorite doorway
You hear plenty about scam texts and suspicious DMs. However, the web remains the leading way scams reach people in Malwarebytes' data. Email came next, followed by SMS.
Malwarebytes says it blocks around 500,000 phishing websites every day. That number gives you an idea of how many fake pages criminals keep pushing online.

Some copy banks or popular retailers. Others imitate technology companies or government services. A link in a text can take you straight to one of these pages. The fake site may look polished enough to fool you at first glance.
So, when a message says something has gone wrong with an account, resist the urge to use the link it provides. Open the company's app yourself or type the website address directly into your browser.
Scam texts hit their peak around lunchtime

Here's the part that really caught my attention. Malwarebytes found that scam texts targeting Americans reached their highest volume around 12 p.m. ET. At noon, volume was about 874% higher than at 1 a.m. ET. Think about what your phone habits look like around lunchtime.

You could be leaving a meeting, grabbing something to eat or checking messages between errands. Your attention may already be split. Then a text arrives saying your package cannot be delivered. Another claims you owe a toll. Maybe a message warns that somebody accessed your account. That timing can work in a scammer's favor because you may react before giving the message a closer look.

Of course, a text arriving at noon does not automatically mean somebody is trying to scam you. The data shows when Malwarebytes observed the highest volume. Still, the pattern gives us another look at how organized scam campaigns have become.
IS THAT TRAFFIC TICKET TEXT A SCAM OR REAL?
A scam text can feel personal and believable even when it comes from an unknown number. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Fridays bring even more scam texts

The day of the week also appears to play a role. Malwarebytes saw its lowest scam text volume on Sunday. Activity then increased as the week went on. By Friday, people were receiving roughly 50% more fraudulent texts than at the beginning of the week.
The researchers cannot say exactly why Friday produced the highest volume. However, the pattern suggests scammers may be deliberately timing campaigns instead of sending messages at random.
Maybe you're finishing work and thinking about the weekend. You could also be juggling deliveries, travel plans or bills. Whatever the reason, criminals want you moving quickly.

That's something we've seen repeatedly with fake government messages. A DMV scam text can threaten fines or license problems while pushing you toward a payment page. The threat gets your attention. The deadline tries to stop you from thinking.
MrBeast is the most impersonated person in the data

Timing gets the message in front of you. Familiarity can make you trust it. Malwarebytes found that Jimmy Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, was the most impersonated person in its data. His likeness appeared in about 30% of impersonation scams observed by the company.

Elon Musk and Donald Trump followed him in the data. These scams can involve fake cryptocurrency giveaways or schemes that demand a fee before you supposedly receive money. The real person has nothing to do with the offer.

Scammers borrow a face you recognize because familiarity can lower your guard. That tactic has become even more troubling as AI-generated video and cloned voices improve. A face on your screen no longer proves the person actually made the video.
Google leads the list of impersonated brands
Scammers use the same strategy with companies you recognize. According to reports from Malwarebytes users, the five most impersonated brands were: Google, Microsoft, Apple, Roblox and Amazon.

Google's name appeared at least twice as often as Amazon's. That familiarity gives criminals a huge advantage. If you use Google every day, a fake security warning may look routine. An Apple customer may react quickly to a message about an account problem.
Amazon scams can land at exactly the right moment because so many of us regularly have packages on the way. So, treat the logo as decoration until you verify the message yourself.
Gaming scams are getting more attention
Gaming communities are also attracting scammers. Malwarebytes found Roblox, Steam, Discord and Minecraft among the most impersonated gaming platforms.
Roblox scam activity increased 15% between mid-June and mid-July. Steam saw a 19% increase during the same period. The potential losses can also get serious.

Malwarebytes says about half of the gaming scams it analyzed could lead to losses of $1,000 or more. That is particularly concerning when younger gamers may encounter fake offers through communities they already trust.
A message promising free in-game items or access to something exclusive can quickly lead to a fake login page. Once the victim enters a password, the scammer may take over the account.
AMAZON JOB SCAM TEXTS ARE SPREADING AGAIN WITH A NEW TWIST
Email scams often start with messages that look routine but hide urgent threats designed to trigger quick clicks. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself from better-timed scams
Scammers can improve their timing, but you can make yourself a much harder target. The best defense starts with slowing down and verifying what you see.

Avoid links and phone numbers inside unsolicited emails, texts or social media messages. A link can take you to a copied website designed to steal your login or payment information. Likewise, the phone number in a fake security alert can connect you directly to the scammer. Instead, leave the message and contact the company another way.

Go directly to the company's official website or open its app. If the message claims you owe money, check your real account before paying anything. You can also contact the organization using a phone number you already trust. This breaks the scammer's control over the conversation.

Searching for a company's website can help, but pay close attention to what you click. Scammers can use sponsored search ads that lead to fake support pages or convincing copies of legitimate websites. Check the web address before entering sensitive information. When possible, use a saved bookmark or the company's official app.

Never give someone your password because they called or messaged you unexpectedly. The same goes for PINs, account recovery codes and one-time verification codes. A scammer may claim they need a code to verify your identity. In reality, that code may give them access to your account. If a caller asks for sensitive information, hang up and contact the organization yourself.

Be suspicious when an unexpected caller or message demands immediate payment. Before paying, confirm the charge through your actual account or by contacting the organization independently. Watch closely for payment requests involving gift cards, cryptocurrency or transfers that may be difficult to reverse. Urgency should make you more cautious, not less.

Strong antivirus software can help block known phishing sites and other malicious pages. Browser protection can also warn you before you enter information on a dangerous website. Keep your browser updated as well. Security updates help close weaknesses that criminals may try to exploit. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Your phone may already include tools that identify suspicious calls or messages. Turn on spam filtering when your device and messaging app support it. Mobile security software can provide another layer of protection by identifying scam texts and dangerous links. No filter catches everything, so continue checking unexpected messages yourself.

If something feels wrong, look into it before you reply. Search for the company's official contact information. Check your account directly. You can also use a reputable scam-checking service to examine a suspicious phone number, message or link. The goal is simple. Verify the claim somewhere outside the conversation the scammer started.

Once you know a message is fraudulent, block the sender and report it as spam. Most phones and email services include built-in reporting options. Reporting scams can also help providers identify campaigns and block similar messages for other users. Then delete the message so you do not accidentally interact with it later.
Act quickly if you already clicked or shared information
If you entered a password on a suspicious site, change it immediately using the real website or app.

Change that password anywhere else you reused it. Better yet, use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account so one stolen password cannot unlock several accounts.
If you gave away payment information, contact your bank or card issuer right away.
You should also review your accounts for unfamiliar activity.
If a scammer gained access to your device, disconnect it from the internet and run a trusted security scan.
Kurt's key takeaways

What grabs me about this research is how deliberate scam campaigns are becoming. Scammers are paying attention to where you spend your time. Now, the timing data suggests they may also be watching when you're more likely to respond. That changes how I think about those random-looking texts that pop up during a busy day. The message may feel like one more thing that needs your attention. That's exactly when you need to slow down. You cannot control when a scammer contacts you. You can control whether that person gets to set the pace. When something unexpected asks for money or account information, get out of the message. Find the real company on your own and check the claim there. That small pause can ruin a scammer's entire plan.
Have you noticed more scam texts arriving around lunchtime or toward the end of the week, and what kind of message almost fooled you into responding? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Cops flush homecoming prank plans after seizing 650 toilet paper rolls in ‘Operation Clean Sweep’
summary: Plainfield police seized 650 rolls of toilet paper in "Operation Clean Sweep" after masked groups targeted homes near Plainfield North High School.
story: Former prosecutor Margaret McLean tells Fox News Digital why police departments are targeting teen takeover organizers before events even happen, warning that these social media-fueled gatherings can turn deadly in an instant.
After warning students not to let homecoming pranks cross the line, an Illinois police department found itself staring down one very unusual haul.
Plainfield police intercepted a massive toilet paper stash allegedly headed for neighborhood homes after reports of masked groups targeting the area near Plainfield North High School.
"And yes… 650 rolls. We counted," police said.

Police displayed the haul under an "Operation Clean Sweep" banner and jokingly gave it an estimated "street value" of $1,708.66 after two nights of escalating complaints from the surrounding community.
TRENDING 'SENIOR ASSASSIN' GAME DRAWS STARK WARNINGS FROM POLICE NATIONWIDE: 'DANGEROUS MISUNDERSTANDINGS'
"Homecoming is not a free pass to damage someone else's property or disrupt their quality of life," the department wrote on Facebook.
FLORIDA POLICE DEPARTMENT GOES VIRAL WITH GENIUS STRATEGY TO CONNECT WITH COMMUNITY

Officers received double-digit calls for service involving teens on both Monday and Tuesday during a two-hour period beginning shortly after 7 p.m. in the area surrounding the high school, according to police.

Residents reported that homes and vehicles had been targeted with toilet paper, eggs, ketchup, detergent pods and other items. Police said groups of 20 to 25 people wearing hoodies and ski masks would "pull up" in several vehicles at the same time and "cause chaos."
STUDENT CHARGED, WEAPON RECOVERED AFTER 3 TEENS TARGETED IN INCIDENT LINKED TO HIGH SCHOOL TRADITION: POLICE

FILE – Toilet paper covers part of a parked vehicle in a file photo. The image is not connected to the homecoming incidents reported in Plainfield, Illinois. (Matthias Balk/picture alliance via Getty Images)
The targets were not limited to friends or classmates. Some of the homes belonged to families with small children or residents with no children at all, police said.
"At this point, we are seeing property damage and significant cleanup, and residents are understandably frustrated," the department wrote.
COPS HALT PLANNED 'TEEN TAKEOVER' AS OFFICIALS BRACE FOR A SUMMER SURGE IN CHAOS AND ARRESTS: POLICE CHIEF
FILE – Rolls of toilet paper are tossed through the air in a file photo. The image does not show the Plainfield homecoming incidents. (Martin Philbey/Redferns)
The department also made clear that the homecoming calls were pulling police attention from more serious incidents.

Officers assisted firefighters at a structure fire, helped Illinois State Police, made a DUI arrest and responded to crashes, intoxicated people, violations of protection orders and a family experiencing a mental health crisis, according to the post.
"In short, we DO have better things to do," police wrote. "So PLEASE, be respectful of your community and let us!"
The department did not say where officers found the toilet paper, whether any arrests were made or whether charges had been filed in connection with the reported damage.

title: California animal rescue operator charged with felonies for alleged 'inhumane and unsanitary conditions'
summary: Video shows the squalid conditions where 300 animals were found at Christine De Anda's unlicensed Los Angeles County kennel, leading to 35 charges.
story: A California woman faces 35 counts and up to 24 1/2 years in prison after authorities uncovered 300 starving, neglected animals at the "Rock 'N' Pawz" facility in Los Angeles County. (KTTV; Los Angeles District Attorney's Office)

A California animal rescue operator is facing up to 24 1/2 years in state prison after being charged with 35 felonies and misdemeanors for alleged cruelty to animals, as she is accused of leaving roughly 300 animals living in severe squalor.

Christine De Anda, 57, operator of the "Rock ‘N’ Pawz" rescue, faces 12 felony counts of animal cruelty, two felony counts of grand theft of labor, and 21 misdemeanor charges ranging from failure to provide care to operating an unlicensed kennel, according to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office.
Prosecutors requested that her bail be set at $914,500 ahead of her arraignment at the Antelope Valley Courthouse.
FLORIDA MAIL CARRIER ACCUSED OF SNATCHING PETS ON ROUTE, TRAPPING 100-PLUS CATS AND DOGS IN ‘HOARDING’ HOUSE

More than 300 animals at the Lake Hughes, California, Rock ‘N’ Pawz animal rescue are alleged to have been forced to live in inhumane and unsanitary conditions, including animals suffering from dehydration, severe injuries and starvation. (Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office)

"For someone who calls herself an animal rescuer, there’s a fundamental responsibility to protect and care for the animals entrusted to her," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said. "Instead, purported rescuer Christine De Anda allegedly left these animals to suffer or die from starvation, dehydration, untreated injuries and painful urine and fecal burns in filthy conditions."

"After repeated citations and warnings, Ms. De Anda continued taking in animals she could not care for, leaving hundreds to endure prolonged suffering," Hochman added. "These animal victims cannot speak for themselves and look to us to protect them. My office will hold their victimizer fully accountable for her inhumane actions."

The charges stem from a March 20, 2026, search warrant executed by Los Angeles County Animal Care and Control (DACC). Investigators removed more than 300 animals — primarily dogs, but also cats, a pig, a rabbit, a goose and two goats — in what DACC Director Marcia Mayeda called the "largest companion animal search warrant and rescue operation ever conducted" in the department’s history.
117 DEAD DOGS FOUND AT ANIMAL RESCUE, MANY WITH GUNSHOT WOUNDS AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE FOR ANSWERS

The operator of Rock ‘N’ Pawz animal rescue in Lake Hughes, California, is also accused of violating multiple county codes, including operating an animal kennel without required land-use approval, maintaining unsanitary conditions and having structures with unpermitted construction, plumbing, electrical and grading work. (Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office)

"More than 300 animals were removed from severely inhumane conditions," Mayeda said. "Animals were living in and saturated with their own excrement, had serious untreated illnesses and injuries, were emaciated, and were forced to live in small crates without adequate room to properly lie comfortably. Our teams have worked tirelessly to stabilize them, provide the medical care they needed, and help them recover."
At least one cat was found dead from starvation and dehydration at the start of the investigation, authorities said.

title: Police officer, woman shot near Notre Dame after football tailgates

story: South Bend authorities detail the chaotic post-tailgate fight that led to one bullet striking a woman and hitting an officer, potentially with shrapnel. (WSBT)
A single gunshot during a post-tailgate fight near Notre Dame's South Bend, Indiana, campus struck a woman and a police officer Saturday night, authorities said.

The violence erupted around 7:30 p.m. ET just as crowds were leaving the university's tailgating areas and heading toward Eddy Street Commons. According to South Bend authorities, Notre Dame Police told them a male suspect was seen armed and reportedly pointing a gun at people, but when South Bend Police found a suspect matching their description, the person was unarmed.

"As approximately 20 South Bend Police Officers were working in Eddy Street Commons and responding to that call, a single gunshot was heard near Eddy Street and Angela Boulevard," South Bend Police said in a Facebook post.
The post said officers soon found a woman with a non-life-threatening leg wound, and a South Bend Police officer with an injury from either a ricochet or shrapnel.

Eddy Street Commons near the Notre Dame campus was shut down for a police shooting investigation Saturday night. (WSBT)
Both victims were transported to a local hospital and are expected to make full recoveries. Police said the officer was "doing fine," and that the woman was "okay."

Notre Dame officials said the suspected shooter fled west from the scene, NBC 5 Chicago reported. The suspect reportedly remains at large. and was described as a heavyset Black male with dreadlocks, wearing blue shorts, a black shirt with a red and blue design on the front, and missing one shoe, according to the local report.
Police are still looking for a shooter who hit a woman and a police officer with a single gunshot after officers were called to a fight at Eddy Street Commons in South Bend, Indiana. (WSBT)

title: Florida plastic surgeon accused of killing attorney in his office defends himself in murder trial
summary: Tomasz Kosowski represents himself in a death penalty trial for the alleged murder of attorney Steven Cozzi, whose body was never recovered.
story: Tomasz Kosowski, the plastic surgeon accused of murdering Pinellas County attorney Steven Cozzi, represents himself in his trial. (FOX 13 Tampa)

An unusual trial is underway for a Florida plastic surgeon, accused of murdering an attorney he’d opposed in court and disposing of his body in a dumpster before prosecutors say it ended up at the landfill.

Clad in an orange jail jumpsuit, Dr. Tomasz Kosowski, 47, is representing himself in court as he faces a first-degree murder charge with the possibility of the death penalty. He’s waived his right to a jury – the judge presiding over the Pinellas County trial is set to decide the doctor’s fate.
Kosowski was arrested in March 2023 in connection with the disappearance of attorney Steven Cozzi. He has remained in jail and insists he is innocent.
The two men met through a legal dispute.
Tomasz Kosowski was accused of killing Steven Cozzi. (Pinellas County Sheriffs Office)
FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON MAY HAVE MURDERED MISSING LAWYER IN LAW FIRM BATHROOM: POLICE

Cozzi had worked on a civil lawsuit beginning in 2019 involving money allegedly owed to Kosowski for work he’d done tied to personal injury cases. Cozzi helped represent the corporate clients Kosowski was suing.

During years of litigation, Kosowski developed a hostile attitude toward Cozzi, according to court records. He blamed Cozzi for his problems in the case and demanded that the attorney be removed as defense counsel, records show.
"He made a bunch of completely unwarranted, inappropriate accusations about Steve throughout the litigation," said Jake Pillsbury, an attorney who worked with Cozzi on the case.
Cozzi had told others that, during a deposition, Kosowski approached him in a restroom and "called him a scumbag" and "that he [Kosowski] was going to win," Pillsbury said in court.
Those close to Cozzi began to worry about his safety.
Cozzi’s husband, Michael Montgomery, had suggested arranging for "some kind of on-site security," if Cozzi had to meet with Kosowski again.
Blood-spattered discovery
On March 21, 2023, Cozzi and Kosowski both were scheduled to attend a teleconference hearing at 10 a.m.
Before that, it was a normal Tuesday morning, Montgomery said. Cozzi brought him his morning coffee and they had a short conversation before he left for work. That was the last time he’d see him.
About 10 minutes before the meeting, Cozzi left his phone, keys, wallet, and other items on his desk and went to the office restroom.
He never showed up for the scheduled teleconference.
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS
Later, Cozzi’s boss entered the restroom and found spattered blood, court records show.
Security footage from the day Cozzi disappeared shows a subject arriving in a silver Toyota Tundra around 8:30 a.m. The prosecution alleges it was Kosowski.
A man wearing dark gloves entered the building where Cozzi worked carrying a box "large enough to conceal a human body," according to investigators.
Steven Cozzi vanished in Florida. Tomasz Kosowski was charged with his murder. (Largos Police Department)
At 10:22 a.m., the same man exited the building pulling a wagon covered with a reddish orange blanket.
The man could be seen struggling with the weight of the cart while pulling it to the truck, records show.

That day, the Tundra was driven to Kosowski’s home in Tarpon Springs, Florida, videos pieced together from multiple surveillance cameras showed, according to court records.

On the way, the truck passed a Flock camera that captured an image of "a red bag or blanket in a cart that appeared to contain what resembles a human body located in the bed of the truck," according to arrest records.

Two days later, investigators arrived at Kosowski’s home with a search warrant and found the Tundra in the garage with blood in the truck bed, on the driver’s side headrest, on the driver’s side floorboard and on the garage floor.
Cozzi’s DNA was found in the Tundra and Kosowski’s garage floor, court records show.

In the search of Kosowski’s vehicles, investigators found a ballistic vest with a "substantial amount" of blood on it. They also found one iPhone and a "burner phone"––the term for an inexpensive, prepaid device meant to be discarded.
Tomasz Kosowski represents himself during his murder trial. (FOX 13 Tampa)

Law enforcement officials also found a vest meant to be worn by a medical first responder, sheriff's office patches, a foldable bike, a gas can, $282,000 in cash, two passports and black, industrial-sized garbage bags.
Investigators also found a black duffel that the prosecution has called "a murder bag." Inside, there were lighters, a Taser, scissors, brass knuckles, a crowbar, ski masks and a Guy Fawkes mask.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
The bag also contained a syringe, a needle and a vial of succinylcholine, a paralytic drug. It was labeled in a way that connected it to Kosowski’s plastic-surgery office in Miami.
Surprising maneuvers caught on video
After Kosowski was arrested, police informed him they’d be searching his body to collect possible DNA and fingernail clippings, and would be taking photographs of him, the prosecution said.
After that, camera footage from inside the patrol car shows Kosowski struggling to bring his hands from behind his back, underneath his feet and up to his face.
He then began to "meticulously suck on each of his fingers," a member of the prosecution team told the judge.

"He's using his tongue and getting up underneath it and slurping. He's using his teeth almost as a nail file, trying to destroy any trace of evidence that might bring him back to Steven Cozzi."
The prosecution argues that Kosowski began planning the killing long before he allegedly murdered Cozzi.
Authorities say Steven Cozzi was killed at this law office in Florida. (Google Maps)
More than a month before the attorney’s disappearance, Kosowski allegedly visited Cozzi’s home without his knowledge and photographed a car in the carport, according to the prosecution team.
Kosowski also visited Blanchard Law Firm where Cozzi worked. He drove around the building and took photos multiple times before Cozzi’s disappearance, the prosecution has alleged.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
In early March 2023, Kosowski began searching Cozzi and Montgomery online, seeking information about their wedding and records about previous and current addresses, prosecutors said.
An employee of the building that housed the Blanchard Law Firm told investigators that a week before Cozzi’s disappearance, she found a man in a mask hiding in the office utility closet.
Suspicious, she asked him why he was there, court records show. He told her it was because of a power outage and walked away.
She watched him leave in a grey Toyota Tundra, investigators said.
Fingerprints matching Kosowski’s were later found in that closet.
Investigators never found Cozzi’s body.
Attorney Steven Cozzi was killed in his Florida law office, authorities say. (St. Petersburg Bar Association)
Searching for Cozzi

On the day Cozzi disappeared, Kosowski’s cellphone was allegedly tracked traveling toward his second home in Miami. He pulled off on a dirt road in South Florida near the Everglades where there’s a dumpster, court records show.

Records of his cellphone’s location show he returned to the dumpster two days later, the prosecution alleges. The team argues that Kosowski returned to the garbage collection container to see if it had been emptied.
Law enforcement later investigated the dumpster and a K-9 trained in human detection alerted on it, indicating the presence of human remains. But a body was not found.
Investigators tracked down the garbage truck driver who collected that dumpster on his route. He remembers that day.
"It was a smell that he had never experienced," a member of the prosecution team told the court.
"He described that smell as vile. He had to crush the trash back in his garbage truck so many times, because the stench was so overwhelming––and this is someone who is a garbage truck driver."

The day he drove that load, the garbage truck driver stopped at a store to buy air freshener because he "could not stand the scent that was in his nose while he was driving around," the prosecution said.
That smell was "Steven's body decaying in the Florida heat for two days."

Video captured by a camera mounted on the garbage truck captured the load from the dumpster tumbling into the truck. That footage shows "a lot of black industrial-sized garbage bags, similar to the ones that Dr. Kozowski had in the trunk of his car," a prosecution team member told the judge.
Video shown in court shows bags falling into the truck that are "consistent with a human body," the prosecution team said.
Law enforcement officers visited the landfill where the garbage truck dumped that load, but it was more than a week after it was deposited.
By that time, more than 6,000 tons of compacted garbage had been piled atop the load.
GOT A TIP?
Still, in an attempt to recover the body of Cozzi, they sifted through the landfill for days, officers testified in court.
"His hearse was a dump truck, and his burial site… is at the Collier County Landfill," a prosecutor told the court.
The prosecution team has called dozens of witnesses to testify before Judge Joseph Bulone.
In July 2025, a written plea of not guilty was submitted by an attorney representing Kosowski at the time. In that plea, he requested a trial by jury.
More than a year later, on Aug. 31, Kosowski told the court he’d changed his mind and wanted a judge to decide his fate.
His trial began on Sept. 14.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

For the first three days of the trial, Kosowski sat mostly quiet, blandly staring at witnesses, taking notes and giving short answers to questions from the judge. On the fourth day, he began cross-examining some of the prosecution’s witnesses who had presented evidence.
He has objected to evidence obtained from his body, from his Toyota Corolla and from his residence, according to court records. His motions to suppress the evidence were denied.

On Sept. 18, the fifth day of his trial, he asked the judge to strike a key witness’s testimony about DNA evidence. He argued that the witness, a DNA expert, didn’t provide enough of his own interpretation of the numbers.
Bulone denied the motion, but said Kosowski could challenge the DNA findings in closing arguments.
Fox News Digital was not able to reach Kosowski for comment.

The trial is set to resume on Sept. 22.

title: Alleged killer mom Corie Walsh ruled too dangerous to return home — but psychiatrist warns risk can change
summary: Forensic psychiatrist explains why a "dangerousness" finding isn't permanent for Corie Walsh, the Illinois mother held without pretrial release.
story: Northwestern's Dr. Stephen Dinwiddie discusses psychosis, dangerousness and why severe mental illness is often misunderstood, particularly in the case of Illinois mom Corie Walsh.

An Illinois judge found Corie Walsh too dangerous to release after prosecutors alleged the Frankfort mother posed a threat to her husband and three surviving children after she was charged with murdering her 2-year-old son, Barrett.
But forensic psychiatrists say "dangerousness" is not a permanent label. Instead, it is a forward-looking assessment that can change as a person's mental condition improves through treatment.
Walsh, 40, remains held without pretrial release after a Will County judge denied her request to leave custody during a detention hearing earlier this month.
LINDSAY CLANCY FIXATION AND ALLEGED PLOT TO POISON HUSBAND EMERGE AS ACCUSED MOM CLAIMS PSYCHOSIS

The judge also ordered that Walsh immediately receive psychiatric medication after her attorneys said she had gone days without treatment despite a hospital recommendation that she receive around-the-clock psychiatric care.

Corie A. Walsh, 38, in a booking photo provided by law enforcement. Prosecutors are asking a judge to deny her pretrial release following the death of her 2-year-old son. (Will County Detention Facility)

Prosecutors argued Walsh should remain behind bars because, beyond the allegations surrounding Barrett's death, she allegedly threatened to kill her husband after her arrest. The judge agreed, finding Walsh posed too great a danger to release before trial.
LINDSAY CLANCY’S FUTURE COULD REST WITH ‘PROSECUTION DOCTORS’ AS CASE ECHOES INFAMOUS MAINE KILLINGS: EXPERT
The ruling raised a broader question that extends beyond Walsh's case: What does it actually mean when a judge determines someone is too dangerous to release?
Under Illinois law, judges deciding whether a defendant should remain jailed before trial evaluate the person's current risk to others rather than punish past conduct.

Dr. Stephen Dinwiddie, a professor of psychiatry at Northwestern University with four decades of forensic psychiatry experience, said psychiatrists approach dangerousness the same way – as a forward-looking assessment rather than a permanent label.
VIRGINIA MAN ACQUITTED BY INSANITY IN KILLING FLEES US DURING 48-HOUR MENTAL HOSPITAL PASS

"Obviously we're talking more about what we're afraid they're going to do tomorrow," he said. "Part of that prediction is based on what they did yesterday... what they did in the past... and what they have said they intend to do."
Corie Walsh, right, poses with her husband and children inside a church. Walsh faces three counts of first-degree murder in the death of her 2-year-old son, Barrett. (Facebook/Corie Walsh)
Unlike a criminal verdict, which looks backward at what allegedly happened, dangerousness is designed to evaluate the risk a person may pose going forward, Dinwiddie said.
"It's pretty squishy," he said. "Dangerous to whom? Imminently or long-term? Dangerous in a physical way or something else?"
In civil commitment proceedings, judges often decide whether someone should receive treatment over their objections because they present a short-term danger to themselves or others.
Dinwiddie said the rationale is simple: "If we don't act, something bad is going to happen within a matter of days, if not sooner."
Dinwiddie said treatment can dramatically change how psychiatrists evaluate a person's future risk.
Police tape surrounds the Frankfort, Illinois, home where officers found an unresponsive 2-year-old boy. (Fox 32 Chicago)

title: Missouri woman federally indicted over chilling death threats allegedly sent to Austin Metcalf's family
summary: Sharifa Nicole Henderson faces a federal indictment after allegedly sending death threats to Austin Metcalf's family after Karmelo Anthony's conviction.
story: Newly released surveillance video shows Karmelo Anthony fleeing from the scene of the crime immediately after the stabbing of Austin Metcalf April 2, 2026.
A Missouri woman was federally indicted in Texas after allegedly threatening the family of Austin Metcalf after Karmelo Anthony's conviction in the teenager's killing.

Sharifa Nicole Henderson, 34, was arrested in Kansas City Sept. 11, two days after a federal grand jury in the Eastern District of Texas indicted her on three counts of interstate threatening communications.
Anthony's trial concluded June 9, and prosecutors allege Henderson made three separate death threats against the Metcalf family in the days that followed.

On June 10, Henderson sent a message through Facebook Messenger to one of the Metcalf family members saying she would kill them and put them in a body bag before stating, "now this is a threat take me to court [expletive]," according to the indictment.

Jeff Metcalf with his son, Austin Metcalf, a junior at Memorial High School in Frisco, who was stabbed in the chest by then 17-year-old Karmelo Anthony, a student-athlete from Frisco Centennial High School. (Courtesy Jeff Metcalf)

Again on June 10, Henderson called the Collin County government, which prosecuted the case against Anthony, and said she would "demolish" the Metcalf family and "strangle" one of them, according to the indictment.
And on June 11, prosecutors say, Henderson sent another threatening message on Facebook Messenger to a family member.

"Don't worry I'll kill you next," she allegedly wrote, according to the indictment. "I will hunt you forever until I kill you...I will be there. You will always have to look over your [expletive] shoulder."
If convicted, Henderson faces up to five years in prison for each charge.

The case drew national attention and became racially charged, with supporters of Anthony criticizing the lack of Black jurors and calling for his acquittal, while supporters of the Metcalf family gathered outside the courthouse seeking justice.
Anthony, 19, was convicted more than a year after fatally stabbing Metcalf, 17, during a regional high school track meet at Kuykendall Stadium in Frisco, Texas, April 2, 2025.
Anthony, then a Centennial High School student, made his way over to the Memorial High School team's tent and sat under it, according to investigators.

Supporters of Austin Metcalf and Karmelo Anthony clash outside the Collin County Courthouse in McKinney, Texas, before a verdict is announced in Anthony's murder trial June 9, 2026. Authorities would later say they found no evidence suggesting the two knew each other prior to the incident.

title: Clancy holdout juror taps former Trump lawyer to fight back as he’s ‘dragged through the mud’: attorney
summary: Michael P. Desronvil, the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial, has retained Edward Paltzik, a lawyer known for representing Trump.
story: Mark Astor, a former prosecutor and behavioral health law expert, tells Fox News Digital that the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy case retaining an attorney signals he needs to 'stand up for himself.'

The lone juror whose holdout forced a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case has retained a lawyer who once represented President Donald Trump, the attorney said. One legal scholar following the case said the move signals the juror is ready to "stand up for himself."

Clancy, 36, faced three counts of first-degree murder in the slayings of her children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — who were discovered strangled at the family's home in January 2023.
Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4 after jurors could not agree on a unanimous verdict, with the panel split 11-1.
Attorney Edward Paltzik told Fox News Digital Friday that he is representing the holdout juror, Michael P. Desronvil.
LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM
Michael P. Desronvil, the juror whose refusal to join the other 11 led to a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial (Fugitive TV)

Desronvil, the lone dissenter from the jury, has come forward and said he didn't stray from his belief that prosecutors proved Clancy was criminally responsible in killing her three children in January 2023 in a statement first reported by NewsNation that was confirmed by Paltzik to Fox News Digital.

"I didn't have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present," Desronvil said. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned."

Paltzik represented Trump in his lawsuit against The New York Times, which he said falsely cast his business success as fraudulent ahead of the 2024 presidential election. The lawsuit was dismissed in 2025 but has since been refiled.
Lindsay Clancy in Plymouth County Superior Court (Pool)

Paltzik was also involved in Trump's lawsuit against CBS after "60 Minutes" was accused of selectively editing an interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. In July 2025, Paramount Global agreed to pay $16 million, which the company said would go toward Trump's future presidential library.
Paltzik said at the time that the CBS interview generated confusion and "mental anguish" among viewers, misled voters and diminished attention to Trump and his online platform, Truth Social.
He also represented Trump during his lawsuit against ABC News, which settled for $15 million and the funds going toward his future presidential library.

Michael P. Desronvil, the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, which ended in a mistrial (Fugitive TV)

In another high-profile case, Paltzik is representing three friends of Nolan Wells. Wells, 18, went missing July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. Crews searched the area for two days before a National Parks Service ranger found his remains on the island's northwestern tip July 6.
Paltzik began representing the friends of Wells in August after several social media influencers made false allegations about them.

"We are proud to stand with and fight for three completely innocent young men: Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo, and Morgan Seymour. Starting today, those who wish to continue trafficking in lies about these Good Ocean Springs People will be held accountable to the maximum extent of the law. We, on the other hand, will be focused solely on the truth, which is that these innocent young men had nothing whatsoever to do with the tragic death of Nolan Wells," Paltzik said alongside Tyler Cox, a Mississippi-based attorney, in a statement to Fox News Digital.
Paltzik said Desronvil won't be doing any other media interviews at this time, calling him an "American Hero" and "Champion of Justice."
LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE
Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

"Again, we are focused entirely on his health, safety, and well-being. There will be a time for accountability and a time for the real story of the Lindsay Clancy Trial to be told. But not right now," Paltzik said on X. "This American Hero and Champion of Justice thanks all of you who have stood by him for your kindness, prayers, and support," he added.

The statement was made as Plymouth County prosecutors weigh whether to retry Clancy, while her attorneys have also raised the prospect of resolving the case without a second jury trial.

Mark Astor, a former prosecutor and behavioral health law expert, told Fox News Digital it's clear Desronvil has retained counsel to "stand up for himself."

"I think there's certainly some indication that his name and reputation is now being dragged through the mud," Astor said. So, I mean, I think he feels like he needs to, you know, at least stand up for himself."

Lindsay Clancy in court last month (Boston Globe via Getty Images)

title: Hasan Piker calls Bin Laden a ‘spoiled brat,’ labels 9/11 ‘blowback’ in Axios interview
summary: Hasan Piker called Osama bin Laden a "spoiled brat" and labeled 9/11 blowback for U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East and Afghanistan.
story: Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin reports on backlash facing Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed after far-left streamer Hasan Piker claimed that America is worse than al Qaeda on ‘America Reports.’

Hasan Piker, the internet streamer and YouTube personality known for his progressive commentary, called Osama bin Laden a "spoiled brat" for his reasoning in orchestrating the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, which he called "blowback" for U.S. actions in the Middle East in the preceding years.

Speaking with Axios, Piker discussed bin Laden's remarks about why he targeted the United States: U.S. support of Israel, American oil policies and U.S. bases in the Middle East. He noted that bin Laden was once a U.S. ally when the U.S. trained, funded and armed the mujahideen in Afghanistan during the Soviet-Afghan War.

"The action was so heinous and so violent that — and also … given his position as formerly an American ally — I think that he came across a little bit more as a spoiled brat that wasn't getting his way. With many backers in the Saudi kingdom as well and the royal family," Piker said.

title: ICE officer accused of lying to FBI about Minneapolis shooting pleads not guilty
summary: Christian Castro pleaded not guilty to six federal charges in the shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis during a Minneapolis immigration operation.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman reports from Dallas on a federal judge blocking attempts by Minnesota to extradite ICE agent Christian Castro from Texas. Castro faces charges stemming from the January shooting of a Venezuelan migrant during Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott investigates whether the officer legally qualifies as a fugitive.

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of lying to the FBI about a January shooting in Minneapolis pleaded not guilty Friday to six federal counts of making materially false statements.

Christian Castro appeared in a federal courtroom in St. Paul after prosecutors accused him of shooting 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg through the front door of a Minneapolis home during Operation Metro Surge.
Castro told investigators he was being attacked with a broom and shovel before opening fire, but prosecutors say surveillance footage contradicted his account.

During his court appearance Friday, Castro, 52, was wearing an ankle monitor and was instructed by a judge to travel only between Minnesota and South Texas. If he has any altercation with law enforcement, he is required to report it within 72 hours, the judge said. He was then released.
ICE OFFICER PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO LYING ABOUT MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING INVOLVING VENEZUELAN MAN

Christian Castro, right, an immigration officer accused of shooting a Venezuelan man during an immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year and lying to investigators, leaves with attorney Daniel Gerdts after a hearing at the Warren E. Burger Federal Building Friday in St. Paul, Minn. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt)

Castro was previously held in Texas custody for about 90 days before he was released. He was held for so long partly because Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities.
Castro was booked in Minnesota last week following his release in Texas, his home state. Upon his release there, Castro was required to wear an ankle monitor and to surrender his passport and guns.
He faces federal and state charges related to the shooting.
ABBOTT TAUNTS FAR-LEFT AG WITH FIERY WARNING OVER ICE EXTRADITION FIGHT: 'SUCH BAD LAWYERS'
Christian Castro is charged with lying to investigators about a January 2026 shooting. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt)

Prosecutors said Castro lied about the circumstances of the shooting, which occurred during Operation Metro Surge, part of the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration. He said he was being attacked with a broom and shovel before he fired his weapon.
The law enforcement operation saw thousands of federal agents in Minnesota that resulted in sweeping arrests, as well as the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, left, and Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, right, battled on X over whether an ICE agent involved in a recent shooting in Minneapolis should be extradited to Minnesota. (Getty Images)

Minnesota authorities have battled the Trump administration over who should handle any charges against Castro. The administration contends that only federal authorities have jurisdiction over the case.

title: Judge Judy warns of 'danger' if prosecutors don't retry Lindsay Clancy after murder trial ends in mistrial
summary: Judge Judy Sheindlin says there's a "danger" in not retrying Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children.
story: Criminal defense attorney Donna Rotunno weighs in on the Lindsay Clancy murder case following a mistrial. They discuss the potential for a plea deal on 'Fox & Friends Weekend'. They debate whether a second trial is likely or if a plea bargain will resolve the charges after the deaths of her three children.

Judge Judy Sheindlin weighed in Thursday on the closely watched Lindsay Clancy murder case following its mistrial, warning there could be a "danger" in prosecutors deciding not to retry the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children.
The 83-year-old judge and television personality was asked by TMZ whether Clancy should face another trial after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict earlier this month.
"I think there's a danger in that, in not retrying," Sheindlin responded.

Sheindlin, who launched the popular syndicated show "Judge Judy," which aired for 25 seasons, was also asked about her view on the outcome of the trial after the jury's deliberations ended in a reported 11-1 split in favor of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.
PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL
"I can't give you a two-minute answer on that," Sheindlin said.
She was then asked whether she believed Clancy should have been found guilty.
"There's no question, my dear, that she killed her children," Sheindlin said. "The only question is, is there an excuse for it? Make up your own mind on that one."
DR PHIL SAYS LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL A 'TEACHABLE MOMENT' ON POSTPARTUM PSYCHOSIS: 'THERE WAS A FAILURE HERE'

Kevin Reddington, defense attorney for Lindsay Clancy, and Lindsay Clancy look on as Judge William Sullivan (out of frame) instructs the jury to continue deliberating, during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on September 4, 2026. ( )
TMZ also asked Sheindlin about Rep. Nancy Mace's public call for Clancy to be publicly executed.
"I think it's ridiculous," Sheindlin responded.
Clancy's defense does not dispute that the 36-year-old former delivery room nurse strangled her three children with exercise bands in January 2023.
Her defense has argued that she was not criminally responsible because of mental illness or defect.
LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR DENIES BIAS ALLEGATIONS, WANTS 'CONVERSATION STARTED' ABOUT WOMEN'S MENTAL HEALTH
Judge Judy Sheindlin warned there could be a "danger" in prosecutors deciding not to retry Lindsay Clancy following the Massachusetts mother's mistrial. (Unique Nicole/Getty Images)
Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4 after seven days of deliberations when jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict.
Several jurors later said 11 members of the panel favored finding Clancy not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, while one favored conviction.

Immediately after the mistrial was declared, Clancy's longtime defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, signaled that he would fight another attempt to put her on trial. The defense has indicated it plans to argue that the circumstances surrounding the mistrial should bar a second trial.

However, in a recent interview with Fox News' Bryan Llenas, Reddington said that if prosecutors reduced the top charge to second-degree murder, he would opt for a bench trial — one without a jury — in the hope that she would receive probation.

title: Top DOJ official warns of deadly smuggling route after 42 vanish at sea
summary: The Justice Department says 42 people vanished at sea after a Colombian smuggler guided them onto a boat from San Andrés Island to Nicaragua.
story: Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva details the deadly smuggling conspiracy tied to 42 people who vanished at sea and warns transnational criminal networks that the Justice Department will chase them wherever they operate.

A Colombian smuggler’s guilty plea is shedding new light on a deadly route to the United States after a boat carrying 42 people vanished at sea and a top Justice Department official said the danger would not have ended if they reached land.

Luis Enrique Linero Pinto, 41, also known as "El Calvo," pleaded guilty in federal court in El Paso, Texas, after being extradited from Colombia for his role in a smuggling conspiracy that prosecutors said used bribery and maritime routes to move migrants north.
The boat left Colombia’s San Andrés Island for Nicaragua on Oct. 21, 2023, carrying approximately 40 migrants and two captains. It never arrived, and no one aboard has been seen or heard from since.
"This was a particularly sad and disturbing situation," Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva, who leads the Justice Department’s Criminal Division, told Fox News Digital.
OVERCROWDED MIGRANT VESSEL WITH 240 PEOPLE ON BOARD INTERCEPTED NEAR TURKS AND CAICOS

A Colombian officer stands beside Luis Enrique Linero Pinto, who pleaded guilty to participating in a human smuggling conspiracy tied to a boat that vanished with 42 people aboard. (The Department of Justice)

"These 40 individuals and the two boat captains, once they set out from San Andrés Island to Nicaragua, were never heard from again," Duva said. "These individuals are, of course, missing and presumed dead, and it appears that there were no survivors."
ELEVEN INDICTED IN ALLEGED TEXAS SMUGGLING SCHEME THAT LEFT 7 MIGRANTS DEAD IN SHIPPING CONTAINER

Duva said the disappearance offers a brutal look at the danger posed by transnational smuggling organizations that turn vulnerable migrants into commodities while pursuing routes toward the United States.
"It’s all about money," he said. "Anybody who’s involved with a cartel or transnational smuggling in this regard, it is about money. It’s about preying on people’s misfortune."
MEXICAN NATIONAL SENTENCED IN BORDER CHILD SMUGGLING CASE INVOLVING THC-LACED CANDY

A coastal view of San Andrés Island, Colombia, where prosecutors say migrants boarded boats bound for Nicaragua as part of a human smuggling route toward the United States. (Robert Bonet/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

According to the Justice Department, Linero Pinto advised migrants on how to reach San Andrés Island, personally received them upon arrival, arranged their accommodations and transported them to boats bound for Nicaragua.
From there, the migrants intended to travel through Central America and Mexico before illegally entering the United States, prosecutors said.
CBP JOINS FORCES WITH COAST GUARD TO INTERCEPT 3 SMUGGLING BOATS, APPREHEND 60 PEOPLE OFF CALIFORNIA COAST

Linero Pinto also bribed members of the Colombian navy to obtain real-time intelligence about the positions of patrol vessels between San Andrés Island and Nicaragua, allowing smuggling boats to evade authorities, according to court documents.
He admitted helping smuggle the migrants aboard the boat that vanished in October 2023.
INSIDE UNDERGROUND EL PASO STORM DRAIN SYSTEM BORDER PATROL SAYS CARTELS EXPLOIT TO SMUGGLE ILLEGAL MIGRANTS
Duva said the victims had not even completed the opening stretch of the dangerous route when they disappeared.

"That’s the first leg. They didn’t even finish the first leg here and get to Nicaragua and then try to come north by land," he said. "It’s a really long journey, and it’s full of really bad things that can happen."
DOJ SAYS 11 MIGRANTS INDICTED IN MULTI-STATE SEX TRAFFICKING, DRUG, FIREARMS CASE
The danger, he warned, is not confined to the open water.

Duva said migrants can face treacherous terrain while traveling through South and Central America and across the U.S.-Mexico border. Even those who reach the United States may be trapped by mounting debts and pushed into sex trafficking, he warned.

"You pay money to come to the United States, and then when you get here, the co-conspirators or those involved in the criminal enterprise will say, ‘But now you owe more, and you’re going to work this off in the sex trade,’" Duva said.
Authorities intercept a suspected migrant-smuggling vessel. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

"Cross-border smuggling cases often times just morph right into human trafficking cases," he continued. "The crime sort of changes along the way. The travelers are the ones victimized, and this comes at a significant cost in terms of public safety."

Linero Pinto was charged in October 2024 and arrested in Colombia that December at the request of the U.S. government. He was later extradited to the United States and made his first appearance in federal court in El Paso in December 2025.
He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit alien smuggling and placing lives in jeopardy. He faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison, though a sentencing date has not been set.
‘GHOSTS’ ON FLORIDA HIGHWAYS: ROADSIDE STINGS SNARE 249 ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS, OFFICERS WARN MANY MORE HIDING
A case against alleged co-conspirator Hernando Manuel de la Cruz Rivera Orjuela remains pending, Duva said.

The prosecution is part of Operation Take Back America and was coordinated by Joint Task Force Alpha, the Justice Department-led initiative targeting cartels and other transnational organizations involved in high-impact human smuggling and trafficking.

Duva praised President Donald Trump and his administration for putting a "tremendous focus" on the initiative and providing the Justice Department with additional resources to pursue smugglers, cartels and other transnational criminal organizations.
"We’re super thankful to President Trump," Duva said. "We’re deeply thankful to the White House for that. We’re thankful to Congress for that, and we’re going to keep doing what we’re doing."
President Donald Trump arrives at a rally at Gastonia Municipal Airport, Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026, in Gastonia, North Carolina. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

Duva said funding approved through Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill allowed the Criminal Division to hire additional prosecutors and place experienced attorneys in sections handling the administration’s priorities.

"People think, ‘Well, what is that? What did it do?’" he said. "We’re feeling the effects of that. We’re able to put skilled prosecutors in these different sections to attack these administration priorities."
Duva said the task force is hunting criminal networks along the southern border, maritime routes near Florida and the northern border with Canada.
"We are focusing on these cases at any border that we have," he said.
His warning to smugglers operating beyond America’s borders was blunt.
"Our reach is substantial," Duva said. "We are going to chase these cases no matter where they originate from or where we find them."
Duva said the department’s expanded international partnerships are critical because the criminals behind the operations often believe distance will protect them from prosecution.
"They just think, ‘Well, they catch other people, but they’re not going to get me,’" he said. "You really try to combat that one case at a time."
Joint Task Force Alpha has produced more than 483 domestic and international arrests, over 436 U.S. convictions and more than 371 significant prison sentences, according to the Justice Department.
FIRST TREN DE ARAGUA GANG MEMBER EXTRADITED TO US ON HISTORIC TERRORISM CHARGES APPEARS BEFORE HOUSTON JUDGE
Homeland Security Investigations personnel conduct a maritime operation in this file image. HSI led the investigation into Luis Enrique Linero Pinto’s human smuggling conspiracy. (X/@HSITampa)
Duva said the mission should transcend partisan fights because the networks being targeted threaten migrants and American communities alike.

"It shouldn’t be partisan," he said. "It should be obvious that anybody who’s in the White House, anybody who is in Congress, should be lauding these cases and the work that’s being done by Criminal Division entities like Joint Task Force Alpha."
The Justice Department’s ultimate goal, Duva said, is the "total elimination" of cartels and the criminal organizations profiting from human suffering.
"You do it one case at a time," he said. "We are focused on doing the very best cases that we can for the American people. That’s what we get up every day and think about."
For Duva, however, the vanished boat remains a haunting illustration of why that mission matters.

"I don’t know that I’ve ever heard of anybody who survives that one after several months and a year," Duva said. "It’s super tragic, and hopefully people realize when they hear about this case just how dangerous it is and how important it is that you target these smuggling groups."

title: Psychosis evidence changes everything in Clancy judge's other killer mom case: retired judge
summary: Judge William Sullivan, who declared a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case, also presided over the Latarsha Sanders trial now vacated by the court.
story: Retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu explains why the Supreme Judicial Court's ruling means a future jury could hear thousands of psychiatric records excluded from Latarsha Sanders' first murder trial.

Judge William Sullivan, who drew national attention earlier this month after declaring a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder case, also presided over another closely watched child-killing trial that a retired Massachusetts judge says would look dramatically different if retried.

The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court last month vacated the murder conviction of Brockton mother Latarsha Sanders, ruling jurors were improperly prevented from seeing psychiatric records central to her insanity defense and ordering a new trial.
"They ordered a new trial which will fundamentally change the way the case is going to be tried," retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu told Fox News Digital.
LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN

Latarsha Sanders appears in Plymouth Superior Court during her 2018 murder trial in Brockton, Mass. Massachusetts' highest court later vacated her convictions and ordered a new trial. (Marc Vasconcellos/The Enterprise via AP, Pool)

Sullivan, who presided over Sanders' 2022 trial and later sentenced her to two concurrent life terms without parole, has returned to the national spotlight following the closely watched Clancy trial, which ended in a mistrial after jurors deadlocked over whether Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three children. Like Sanders, Clancy admitted killing her children but argued she lacked criminal responsibility because of mental illness.

"There is no doubt the defendant committed these incomprehensible crimes," Justice David Gaziano wrote for the unanimous court in Sanders' case. "The sole issue before a Superior Court jury was whether she lacked criminal responsibility."
LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE CALLS MISTRIAL, THEN GRANTS DEFENSE ONE HOUR STAY FOR APPEAL

The justices concluded Sanders was entitled to a new trial because jurors never saw medical records documenting diagnoses and treatment of mental illness that were relevant to the only issue disputed at trial: whether she lacked criminal responsibility.
Lu said the ruling does far more than simply order another trial.
"Thousands of pages of mental health records will be admitted ... and the jury's gonna get it all," he said.
Judge William Sullivan speaks during Lindsay Clancy's trial on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)
Lu cautioned against judging Sullivan's decision with the benefit of hindsight.

"The trial judge did an excellent job ... but now I'm a great Monday morning quarterback just like everybody else," Lu said, explaining that the evidentiary issue was unusually difficult before the SJC clarified the law.
Sanders admitted killing her sons, 8-year-old Edson "Marlon" Brito and 5-year-old La'Son Brito, but argued she was legally insane at the time of the attacks.

Her attorneys contended she was suffering from severe mental illness and psychosis, while prosecutors argued she appreciated the wrongfulness of her actions despite bizarre statements she made before and after the killings.
According to evidence summarized by the Supreme Judicial Court, Sanders had become consumed by conspiracy theories involving the Illuminati and expressed fears about voodoo before the killings.
After the deaths, investigators said she gave police multiple conflicting accounts before eventually telling detectives the stabbings were part of a "ritual" tied to voodoo and the Illuminati.

Lindsay Clancy looks on as jurors enter the courtroom during Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on Sept. 4, 2026. (Greg Derr/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
At trial, Sanders' defense called a clinical neuropsychologist who testified she was "grossly psychotic" at the time of the killings and suffered from a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder.
The expert based that opinion in part on thousands of pages of psychiatric treatment records from prison and a state psychiatric hospital.
Those are the records Lu said a future jury would likely hear if prosecutors pursue another trial.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

The Supreme Judicial Court said that was an error, concluding the excluded records documented repeated observations of paranoia, hallucinations, delusional thinking and schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses that formed the medical foundation of Sanders' defense.
Read the court's ruling:

"We hold that the exclusion of the MCI-Framingham and WRCH medical records documenting the defendant's post-arrest diagnoses or treatment of mental illness ... impermissibly stripped the sole defense 'of the medical foundation that supported it,'" the court wrote. "The defendant is entitled to a new trial."
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Lu said the opinion should not be interpreted as a determination that Sanders was legally insane or wrongly convicted. Instead, he described it as the resolution of a difficult evidentiary question that changes what evidence jurors would be permitted to consider if the case is retried.

During oral arguments before the Supreme Judicial Court, Sanders' attorney, Robert Shaw, argued the trial judge's exclusion of medical evidence deprived his client of "a meaningful opportunity to present a complete defense," FOX 25 in Boston reported.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Assistant Plymouth County District Attorney Melissa Johnson countered that Sanders showed no documented psychotic behavior for months after the killings and that the records were properly excluded, the station reported.
SEND US A TIP
The justices also addressed two issues that would likely shape any future trial.
GOT A TIP?

First, they said prosecutors could refer to Sanders describing herself as "evil" because the statements were relevant to whether she appreciated the moral wrongfulness of her actions, so long as the argument remained tied to that legal issue rather than serving as a personal attack.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
However, the court found prosecutors improperly suggested Sanders may have borrowed elements of her story from episodes of "Law & Order: SVU," ruling there was no evidence supporting that theory.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
The ruling vacates Sanders' convictions and sends the case back to Plymouth Superior Court for a new trial.
An overturned conviction does not clear Sanders of the charges, Lu said.
"It just means you have to do it all over again," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital has reached out to Sullivan, Sanders' attorney and the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office for comment.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

title: Minnesota woman's mugshot goes viral after social media users spot resemblance to Jennifer Lopez
summary: A Minnesota woman's mugshot is going viral after social media users spotted what they call a striking resemblance to pop superstar Jennifer Lopez.
story: CNN accidentally aired a photo of Dolly Parton impersonator Kelly Vohnn during a report about the music icon's passing.
The mugshot of a Minnesota woman arrested for allegedly stealing batteries is going viral after social media users noticed her resemblance to a famous pop superstar.

Cyrena Anne Quast, 35, was arrested Aug. 30 on a theft charge in Monticello after she allegedly stole two double packs of power tool batteries valued at around $580 from a store, according to a criminal complaint obtained by TMZ.
But it was Quast's booking photo that had the internet doing a collective double take.
JENNIFER LOPEZ'S BOLD WIMBLEDON HAT DIVIDES FANS OVER ROYAL BOX ETIQUETTE
Social media users debated whether Minnesota theft suspect Cyrena Anne Quast, right, bears a striking resemblance to Jennifer Lopez, left. (KMazur/WireImage; Wright County Sheriff's Office)
Social media users quickly pointed out that the mugshot appeared to bear a striking resemblance to Jennifer Lopez.
"It really does look like her!" one user exclaimed, while others suggested the two could even pass for twins.
Another referenced Lopez's 2002 hit "Jenny from the Block," declaring Quast, "the real Jenny from the block."
Others had a little more fun with the comparison, with one saying Quast looked like J.Lo if the global superstar "had a really rough week."
JENNIFER LOPEZ SENDS FANS INTO A FRENZY AS SHE SHOWS OFF CHISELED ABS IN GYM SELFIES
Cyrena Anne Quast's booking photo went viral after social media users pointed out what they saw as a striking resemblance to pop superstar Jennifer Lopez. (Wright County Sheriff's Office)
Another suggested Quast might have a future as Lopez's stunt double.
Still, not everyone was seeing double, with plenty of social media users pushing back on the supposed "uncanny" resemblance.
"She looks absolutely nothing like her," one user quipped.
Her alleged return visit raised red flags when an employee recognized Quast from a similar theft days earlier and alerted police, according to the complaint.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Jennifer Lopez has been a major presence in Hollywood for more than three decades. (Valentina Frugiuele/Getty Images)
Quast was arrested and booked into the Wright County Jail on a gross misdemeanor theft charge.
