title: Trump administration grants visas to top Iranian leaders to attend U.N. General Assembly
summary: The decision to grant Iranian leaders visas to travel to New York City for the annual meeting of global leaders comes seven months into the U.S. war with Iran.
story: The Trump administration will allow an Iranian delegation to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week, albeit with some restrictions, a State Department spokesperson said Thursday.
The decision to grant Iranian top officials visas to travel to New York City for the annual meeting of global leaders comes seven months into the U.S. war with Iran.

“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend U.N. General Assembly High Level Week,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy.”

The Iranian delegation’s trip comes at a sensitive time, as the U.S. military and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have continued attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the war.
President Donald Trump said Thursday that he is considering resuming full-scale attacks against Iran.
“I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me,” Trump told Axios.
Last week, the U.S. military struck five Iranian tankers linked to the IRGC in response to attempted attacks on an American warship, according to U.S. Central Command.

The Iranian delegation cleared by the U.S. will be smaller than the one the country sent last year, the State Department said. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will be a part of the delegation receiving U.S. visas, a U.S. source familiar with the decision said.

The U.S. has historically restricted the Iranian delegation’s travel during its visits to New York, but beginning in 2025 the Trump administration began blocking the officials’ access even to wholesale and luxury stores, confining their movements to “areas strictly necessary to transit to and from the U.N. headquarters district to conduct their official U.N. business,” according to the State Department.

“We will not let the Iranian regime’s elites exploit UNGA for a luxury retail splurge paid for by the Iranian people’s suffering, all while the regime funnels Iran’s wealth to support its terrorist proxies,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said Thursday on social media. “The U.S. will continue to ban Iranian UN Mission officials, visiting officials, and their dependents from buying wholesale club memberships or luxury goods here.”

Last month, an Iranian presidential protocol official said Tehran was still assessing the level and size of its attendance at the General Assembly this year, calling the conditions imposed by the U.S. illegal, without elaborating on the complaint.

The general debate of the General Assembly, the part of the meeting where world leaders will give speeches, will begin on Tuesday when Trump is expected to speak. Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Wednesday.

Despite granting visas to the Iranian delegation, the Trump administration will once again block Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas from attending the General Assembly, according to a source familiar with the decision.

That decision is an extension of sanctions that deny the necessary visas to officials from the Palestinian Authority and the Palestine Liberation Organization to attend the annual meeting of global leaders, according to the source.

In a statement Wednesday, the State Department accused both organizations of trying to bypass negotiations by seeking unilateral recognition of a Palestinian state, taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict — including through the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice — and “glorifying acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks.”

The Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates rejected the U.S. decision and said in a statement that “the unjustified measure” runs counter to efforts aimed at restoring trust and “creating the political climate necessary to implement the two-state solution and achieve peace and stability in the region.”

title: King Charles issues fiery response to Princess Diana’s brother over claims in new book
summary: In a rare rebuke, Buckingham Palace issued a robust statement aimed at King Charles III’s former brother-in-law, Earl Charles Spencer, as he is set to release his bombshell memoir.
story: LONDON — Buckingham Palace has issued a rare and unusually forceful denial after the late Princess Diana’s brother claimed that the then-Prince Charles said his first wife would soon be forgotten in the days after her death.
In a soon-to-be-published memoir, Charles Spencer recounts the emotional days in the aftermath of Diana’s 1997 death in a Paris car crash at age 36.

An excerpt published Wednesday alleges a heated exchange with Charles, now the British king, over whether Princes William and Harry — then 15 and 12 — should walk behind their mother’s coffin in the funeral procession.

Spencer says he expressed that Diana would not want them to endure such an ordeal and claims that was met with a “stream of anger” from Charles. He writes that Charles “unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’”
Buckingham Palace replied with a forceful statement denying the claims and suggesting that grief for his older sister may have affected Spencer’s memory.

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” said the statement, released Wednesday.
Diana’s 1997 funeral procession is etched into modern memory.
Her brother and two young sons were among those who walked solemnly behind her coffin as it passed through central London.

India McTaggart, a royal correspondent at The Telegraph newspaper, told NBC News about Wednesday’s statement: “Earl Spencer’s book is expected to contain a number of incendiary claims, and perhaps this was the palace trying to get on the front foot and get ahead of some of the allegations we expect to see.”
The royal family mostly avoided commenting in 2023, when Prince Harry published his autobiography, “Spare,” which also generated global headlines with claims of bitter family feuds.

Queen Elizabeth II famously issued a brief but forceful statement in 2021 after Harry and his wife, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, alleged racism in the family. “Recollections may vary,” the late queen said.
McTaggart said that “the palace will certainly be bracing for more headlines” as a result of the new memoir.
Add to Google
Add to Google

“At the same time, we’ll see Harry carrying out public engagements this week, while the king and the prince and princess of Wales continue with theirs. It will be interesting to see how all of that is covered now that they’re all in Britain at the same time.”

Diana was one of the most photographed women in the world after she married Charles in 1981. Their high-profile marriage ended in 1996, and she died a year later after being chased by paparazzi with her partner, Dodi Fayed. Her death in a Paris tunnel brought the world to a standstill.

At the time of her funeral, the royal family received criticism from the public and the media for appearing to be slow to react to the outpouring of love and grief from the public for a woman posthumously dubbed the “people’s princess.”
Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be published Tuesday. Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper is publishing excerpts in advance.

title: Australian athlete apologizes after winning race despite involuntary bowel movement
summary: “Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track,” Hyrox competitor Joanna Wietrzyk said.
story: An Australian athlete apologized Thursday for continuing — and winning — her race in China over the weekend after experiencing an involuntary bowel movement during competition.
Joanna Wietrzyk, a 24-year-old from Melbourne, said she should have pulled off the track during the women’s 16-to-24 Hyrox event in Beijing on Saturday.
The athlete said she hadn’t felt any symptoms before the race that might have warned her about what was to come.
“I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing,” Wietrzyk said in a statement.

“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”

Hyrox is a relatively new indoor sport that combines running and performing high-intensity exercises at various workout stations. It’s not an Olympic sport, but its backers hope it could make the Games in 2032 or 2036.

“I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected,” Wietrzyk said. “I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away.”
Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologized for the incident on Sunday and said organizers should have intervened immediately.
Wietrzyk’s time of 1:01:23 would have put her atop her division, but she has asked to “retroactively withdraw” from competition.

“On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned,” Wietrzyk said. “Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support. It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.”

title: How Canada and the E.U. are teaming up to counter Trump
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg to lay out how middle powers might counteract Trump’s hostility.
story: Around 3,700 miles separate the Gothic towers of Canada’s Parliament in Ottawa from the glass-fronted modern European Parliament building in eastern France.
But judging by the thunderous applause shaking the E.U. chamber Thursday, President Donald Trump’s threats are helping to close that distance.

Canada and Europe have long been close U.S. allies, benefiting from American military power and trading heft. But Trump has upended those relationships, waging trade wars against Canada and the E.U., while threatening to absorb Canada as America’s 51st state and take control of Greenland, Denmark’s autonomous Arctic territory.
Without a reliable partner in the White House, the spurned allies are now forging their own path.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged the world’s “middle powers” to join forces in a speech before the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday to create “an alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices.”
The strategy in short: strength in numbers.
“I’m not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival, only with better manners,” he stressed.

“We do not seek power to dominate others,” Carney continued. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience. So no one — no one — can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

The remarks appeared aimed in part at Trump, though Carney did not name the president in his speech. The response in the room was a near-unanimous standing ovation from lawmakers representing the bloc’s 27 member countries.
Some European leaders, meanwhile, appear ready to grant Canada more favorable access to its closely guarded single market.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen caused a stir Wednesday when she suggested making Canada the E.U.’s first “associate member.” She also outlined an “alliance for the future” that would increase cooperation on defense, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and other tech.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.

At a news conference Thursday, Carney stressed that Canada was “not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member” of the European Union, a long and drawn-out process of regulatory alignment that can sometimes take decades for applicant countries.
“What matters is the substance,” he said of the associate membership proposal.

Carney has deep links to Europe, having served as governor of the Bank of England before his political homecoming propelled him to Canada’s leadership. He tapped into those ties Wednesday, bonding with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at an Everton soccer match.

title: New wild cat species is identified for first time in 100 years, researchers say
summary: Researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science. The Tilcayo tiger cat is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian cloud forest.
story: For the first time in a century, researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science.

Leopardus tilcayo — or the tilcayo tiger cat — is slender and spotted, with rounded ears. It is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian Yungas, the cloud forest where the Andes mountains meet the Amazon basin. The species was described for the first time in the journal Current Biology on Thursday.
Researchers identify new species of wild cat

It’s rare to find a new, relatively large mammal. Unsurprisingly, most newly discovered animal species are small in size, said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who co-authored the study and leads a wild cat conservation program called Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia (Bolivian Felid Research and Conservation Program).
“This time, it’s a cat. That’s really novel. And it hasn’t happened in 100 years,” she said. “No one else had named it. No one else had described it.”
The size of the Leopardus tilcayo population is not clear yet.

“We really don’t know how many cats are still in the wild,” said Nogales-Ascarrunz, whose work as a conservationist is funded by National Geographic. “We need science, we need more studies to answer this question, which is actually critical for its conservation.”

title: U.S. accuses Russia of plot to kill a prominent dissident in Washington
summary: The Justice Department unsealed charges against five people it alleged were part of the Kremlin’s “global assassination network” aimed at causing “destruction and mayhem.”
story: The Kremlin orchestrated a murder-for-hire plot against a prominent Russian dissident in Washington this summer, according to the Justice Department, which unsealed charges against five people it alleges were part of a “global assassination network” aimed at causing “destruction and mayhem around the world.”

The five people are still at large, the Justice Department said in the indictment, which was unsealed late Tuesday, describing the wider operation being run by Russian intelligence as “brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching.”
The FBI said it had disrupted the plot, although officials did not detail how.

Since at least 2024, the network is alleged to have paid Americans and foreigners to spy on targets, “carry out targeted killings” and “commit acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that are aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine,” the Justice Department said.

Asked for a response to the allegations by NBC News, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily briefing call with reporters that “until we have heard or seen any reasonable evidence and arguments based on at least something tangible, we do not consider it necessary to comment on this news.”
Western governments have accused Russia for decades of carrying out attempted and successful killings abroad. Despite substantial evidence, it has always denied the allegations.

The indictment did not name the intended victim in Washington. The Justice Department lists the defendants as Yuri Khrameev, known as “Colonel Yuri,” 63, and his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, both of Russia; Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, known as “Viking,” both 35 and Cuban nationals; and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, of Venezuela.
The indictment describes Durruthy as “an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia,” where, it says, Suarez and Castro also reside.
All face a charge of conspiracy to finance terrorism. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro face an additional charge of conspiracy to commit murder for hire.
Yuri Khrameev is alleged to be a former Russian intelligence colonel, while his son is an officer in Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB.

Prosecutors allege the network recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in Brooklyn, New York, this summer, promising him between $1,000 and $1,500 to photograph and record two locations associated with the Washington target.

The man carried out the surveillance but declined an offer from Suarez and Castro of $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target himself, prosecutors said. The alleged recruiters asked whether he knew somebody who would.
Suarez also offered substantial sums of money to other people in the U.S. to finish the job, the indictment says.

The indictment quotes messages that prosecutors said show the conspirators referred to murder as “construction.” Surveillance instructions included putting the man’s phone into airplane mode and recording while passing the house.
Suarez is alleged to have said that he also had people in Mexico who could carry out the killing but that they were delayed.
Authorities allege a second plot involving a dissident believed to be living in Lithuania whom the network accused of making derogatory statements about Russia.

In that case, a U.S. citizen was promised $200 to photograph the target’s address last year and then was offered around $25,000 to kill him, prosecutors said. When he refused, Yuri Khrameev offered a “simpler job,” prosecutors said — setting fire to a warehouse or attacking an electricity substation.
The purpose, Khrameev is alleged to have said, was to target “all the countries that are helping Ukraine.”
Durruthy, meanwhile, is accused of coordinating logistics for attacks in Prague in June 2024 and Lithuania that September.
Lithuanian authorities publicly named Durruthy as wanted in January in a case involving attempts to burn military equipment intended for Ukraine, according to the Lithuanian broadcaster LRT.

“These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” said John A. Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general for national security.
“Actions like these represent a gross violation of our sovereignty and a threat to our national security,” he said.
James C. Barnacle Jr., head of New York’s FBI office, said the agency “disrupted this operation through relentless work and rock-solid partnership.”

title: Saudi Arabia accuses Houthis of attacking Mecca, warns holy city is a ‘red line’
summary: The Iran-backed Yemeni rebels denied targeting the city in their escalating campaign against the key U.S. ally.
story: Saudi Arabia has accused the Iran-backed Houthi rebels of attempting to attack Islam’s holiest city, declaring Mecca a “red line” in the escalating conflict.
The kingdom’s claim drew condemnation from across the Middle East, but no immediate sign of military support as fears grew of a return to all-out war between the key U.S. ally and the Yemeni rebels.

The Houthis swiftly denied targeting Mecca, saying their operations had targeted Saudi oil facilities and military bases, “far removed” from the sacred site of the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad. They accused Saudi Arabia of spreading “fabrications and lies.”

The Houthis’ rapid ground advance in Yemen and aerial attacks on Saudi Arabia have shut down a crucial oil pipeline, threatened energy supplies through a second major shipping route and left the kingdom struggling to respond.

The mounting hostilities have threatened to open a second front in the Iran war, with oil and gas prices rising.  President Donald Trump has so far offered no sign of any U.S. plans to intervene in this new theater.

The United States on Wednesday upgraded its travel advisory to Saudi Arabia to Level 3 amid the escalating conflict, warning Americans to “reconsider travel” to the kingdom and banning government employees from travel near the Yemen border.

Saudi military spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said Wednesday that the country’s air defense forces had intercepted the drone south of Mecca just before 7 p.m. local time Tuesday (12 p.m. ET), according to a statement.

He emphasized that the security of the holy city and of pilgrims was a “red line,” warning there would be no hesitation to take “necessary and deterrent measures” against the Houthis, the statement said.
Mecca is known as the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, with millions of Muslims from around the world making the pilgrimage to the holy city each year.

“While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia trade barbs over whether the target was Mecca or not,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a think tank based in Washington, D.C., who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, “what is clear is you’re seeing a real demonstration of the Houthis’ continued strategic depth.”
He added: “The fact that they were able to strike this deep in Saudi Arabia is really a signal toward their capacity, if not future intentions.”
The Iran-backed rebels have ramped up attacks on cities across the kingdom after also capturing a key Red Sea port city and island in their bid to gain control of the crucial Bab el Mandeb Strait.

Oil prices have soared over fears that the Houthis could shut down the waterway, which has been a crucial transit route for Saudi Arabian oil exports with the Strait of Hormuz largely closed by Iran since the U.S. and Israel launched their war in late February.
The international benchmark, Brent crude, was at around $108 per barrel early Wednesday. The nationwide average cost of diesel fuel hit another all-time high of $6.31.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the alleged Mecca attack as a “dastardly and heinous” act.
Sharif, who recently reached a joint defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, did not directly mention the Houthis in his statement, but reiterated Pakistan’s general support for the kingdom.
The U.S. conducted a deadly bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, but has shown little appetite for another.

Trump said over the weekend that the Houthis had called his administration and said they “don’t want to fight with us.” Speaking with reporters during a visit to Dublin on Saturday, he said he also spoke with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and maintained that everything would “work out fine and dandy” in the region.
The Houthis and the opposing coalition backing the internationally supported Yemeni government have been fighting a civil war since 2014, with no clear resolution despite a truce agreed years ago.
The United Nations Security Council met Tuesday in an emergency session to discuss the rising violence in Yemen, the region’s poorest country, with member countries urging de-escalation.
The U.N. warned that the ongoing clashes between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Houthi rebels have displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September.

title: Hyrox co-founder apologizes after athlete allowed to continue despite defecating on herself
summary: Professional athlete Joanna Wietrzyk was seen on video and in photographs running and using shared fitness equipment with feces running down her legs.
story: The international indoor sports competition Hyrox apologized after an incident in Beijing where a runner was allowed to continue a race after soiling herself during the event.

Professional athlete Joanna Wietrzyk finished and won the competition on Saturday, which consists of running and high-intensity exercises. The athlete was seen on video and in photographs racing and using shared fitness equipment with feces running down her legs.

Competitors alternate between running a kilometer and performing exercises at workout stations, including sled pushes and pulls, burpees, rowing and lunges while carrying sandbags. Wietrzyk holds a world record in the Hyrox women’s solo event.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste issued a statement Sunday on social media apologizing “to all that were directly or indirectly affected, as well as to everyone who felt like we did not handle the situation like we should have.”
“HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race,” he wrote. “In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not.”
Fürste said Hyrox made changes to its rules and procedures for the event as a result of the incident, but did not elaborate on what those changes were.
“As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again,” he said.

In another statement on social media, the company said: “As our sport continues to evolve we are encountering new and increasingly complex situations that challenge us and where additional clarity is needed.” The statement has since been removed.

“We ask our athletes to push themselves to the highest levels. At times, they will go beyond what even we thought was possible,” the brand said. “That courage, resilience and refusal to give in are precisely what makes elite athletes so extraordinary. Our role is to give them the right framework and the right boundaries within which they can compete, perform and express themselves at their very best.”

The brand said it has “clear biocontaminant and medical procedures in place. In this instance, an unforeseen situation arose in which protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood.”

“We recognise that this can understandably lead to frustration, questions and strong views within our community,” the statement said. “Those concerns are legitimate and, as organisers, we must be prepared to hear them, examine what happened and take responsibility for continuing to improve.”
Hyrox did not immediately respond to requests for comment on why the post was taken down or what specific policy changes were made in response to Saturday’s race.
Wietrzyk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

According to The Guardian, Wietrzyk posted and later deleted an image of herself to her Instagram Story from what appeared to be a hospital bed that read, “Go hard or go home … a win is a win. In all seriousness, thank you for all the support. I’ll be back soon.”

title: U.S. and China face grave AI risks, but mutual distrust stalls cooperation
summary: Foremost among the threats for Beijing is the risk to the ruling Communist Party, which worries the technology could be weaponized against it.
story: BEIJING — The United States and China are both gripped by safety fears as they reckon with their rapid advances in AI, but intensifying competition and deep mutual distrust could derail the kind of cooperation experts say is vital to head off the strategically vital technology’s greatest dangers.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly at the center of the rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and it is expected to be a major topic of discussion at a summit in Washington next week between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

The summit comes as AI leaders and researchers in the U.S. warn that companies should “slow the pace” of AI development, citing recent incidents involving autonomous agents. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must maintain AI dominance over China through export controls and other measures.
How exactly could AI cause widespread danger?

China, which tightly regulates AI and largely avoids the existential worries the technology provokes in the U.S., has interpreted calls to slow its development as targeted squarely at its own progress. U.S. companies say the Chinese AI sector is being driven in part by large-scale “illicit distillation” of their most advanced models.
Chinese officials, who say distillation is a conventional practice that U.S. companies also use on Chinese models, in turn accuse America’s AI executives of trying to stave off competition.
Senior Col. Zhu Qichao, a noted voice on Chinese military AI and national security, called for “cooperation” with the U.S. while warning against “vicious competition.”

“Because with the development of emerging technologies, it definitely comes with many possibilities,” said Zhu, the director of the Institute for Defense Technology and Strategic Studies at the People’s Liberation Army National University of Defense Technology.
“On one hand, it benefits humanity, but on the other hand, there are also considerations regarding risks,” he told NBC News on Tuesday at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing.

AI and the worries around it were a major focus at the annual defense forum, where rooms were packed with scholars, military officials and commentators from the U.S. and other countries, many of which are being pressured to pick sides in the U.S.-China AI race.
Though Trump and Xi agreed at their May summit in Beijing to hold high-level AI talks, no such talks have been publicly confirmed ahead of Xi’s visit next week.
Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, said China was wary that the talks could be used to further slow its progress.

“On the other hand, I think both sides need to sit down to talk about the risks posed by AI development,” he said at the forum, adding that “it will take a long way before the two sides can really forge some important consensus on this issue.”
For U.S.-China cooperation to work, the U.S. needs to be open to both sides benefiting, said Francesca Giovannini, executive director of the Harvard Belfer Center’s Initiative on Managing the Atom.

“The United States operates on a very specific type of theory. And the theory is, whoever wins the AI race wins everything,” she said in an interview at the forum. “So if this is your zero-sum game idea, you won’t be conceding anything.”

China is unlikely to agree to a slowdown at the behest of U.S. AI companies, said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at the Asia Group, an American strategic advisory firm based in Washington.

“I don’t think what happens in the U.S. really matters to China,” he said Tuesday in a phone interview from Hong Kong. “They want to do AI at their own pace, and to a very large degree a lot of people in the industry, in the government, they have a very proud sense that this is finally the chance for China.”

China, which sees its “open-weight” AI models as a tool for diplomacy, has promoted the technology as a global “public good” that should be managed by the international community. At a summit in India on Sunday, Xi offered the 11-member BRICS group of nations help developing open-source AI and urged them to join China’s global AI governance initiative.
But China is also keenly aware of the risks it faces from its own AI success, with Xi telling a Shanghai conference in July that authorities must “ensure that AI is always under human control.”

The industry must make mandatory filings and submit security assessments to officials, with many of the companies having to submit technical filings to an algorithm registry. The government has also imposed rules requiring watermarking and safety requirements.

Foremost among the risks are potential threats to China’s ruling Communist Party, which worries the technology could be weaponized against it and has imposed ideological controls to ensure products fall in line with socialist values, for example.

“Hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives misuse generative AI technologies — such as deepfake audio-video, AI-generated graphics and text, and intelligent bot farms — to manufacture political rumors, spread harmful information, and incite confrontation at low cost and on a massive scale,” Chen Yixin, the Chinese minister of state security, said in an article Sunday in the state-backed China Cybersecurity Magazine that called for greater party control and government oversight of AI.

Chen said AI could enable misinformation campaigns and cyberattacks on China’s critical infrastructure and, in an apparent reference to the U.S., warned that countries with “advantages” in AI could restrict other nations’ access to their technologies.

He also warned of espionage and data leaks, days after Anthropic released a report that found Chinese AI labs had secretly routed requests to its Claude models, some of which contained sensitive information from individuals, major companies and state-affiliated actors.

Like the U.S., China increasingly views AI as a national security issue, down to the individual researchers working on it. On Tuesday, China tightened travel curbs on its citizens, barring some whose work has implications for national technology security from leaving the country.

The new rules add to an extensive AI regulatory regime that includes restrictions on AI companions over mental health concerns, mandated labeling of AI-generated content and a requirement that trained models must use data conforming to Chinese values.

Experts say it could take a major crisis for the U.S. and China to finally work together on AI, much like the 1962 Cuban missile crisis pushed the U.S. and the then-Soviet Union to start negotiating on nuclear weapons.

AI has already had profound military implications, including for targeting, and could be integrated into systems supporting the nuclear chain of command, said David Finkelstein, vice president of the Center for Naval Analyses.
“This is scary stuff, and I think that this is an area where the two sides ought to be sitting down and talking to each other,” he said at the forum.

U.S.-China competition is inevitable, but there is still room for the two sides to negotiate because their respective positions “are not necessarily very much entrenched,” said David Santoro, president and chief executive of Pacific Forum International, a Honolulu-based think tank.
“There are still ways that we can better understand each other and hopefully come up with mechanisms so we can better control this emerging technology,” he said in an interview at the forum.
Santoro said he was “not very optimistic,” however, about the prospect for a major agreement in the near term.
“I don’t know that we will be able to get to a position where we agree on something substantive,” he said. “But at least the first step has got to be talking to each other.”
Eric Baculinao and Erin Tan reported from Beijing and Mithil Aggarwal from Hong Kong.

title: Russia and Ukraine launch new attacks on energy despite Trump’s ceasefire claim
summary: The president’s statement that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to pause strikes against each other’s energy infrastructure was followed by a night of strikes on energy infrastructure.
story: President Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure. Then, overnight into Tuesday, both sides launched new attacks on energy.

Russia fired a volley of 200 drones at Ukraine, hitting energy and port facilities, Ukrainian officials said. In the capital, Kyiv, one person was killed and seven others were injured in attacks on two gas stations, warehouses and other sites, according to local authorities.
In the south and the west, Russian strikes damaged homes, as well as port and transportation infrastructure.

Kyiv’s military, meanwhile, said it struck the Syzran oil refinery in Russia’s Samara region. Ukrainian officials also reported strikes on a drone production facility in Taganrog and a drone preparation and launch site in the Oryol region.
This is the daily reality of Russia’s assault, now in its fifth year, to bomb Ukraine’s military and population into submission.

title: Harry and Meghan change their children’s school over security concerns
summary: Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, were enrolled in an undisclosed school when their parents moved back to Britain from California last month.
story: LONDON — The children of Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, have changed school just days into the new academic year, with the couple citing security concerns.
Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, were enrolled in an undisclosed school when their parents moved back to Britain from California last month.
But just days after they started at the new school, they have now switched to another.

“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” a spokesman for Harry and Meghan said in a statement.

“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family,” the statement added. “This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”
Hello! Magazine first reported the story.
NBC News royal contributor Emily Nash cited specific concerns the couple appeared to have.

The school “was at a fair distance from the place where they’re staying in the U.K. and they weren’t able to properly protect themselves in heavy traffic,” Nash, who is also royal editor for Hello! Magazine, said in an interview.
“On the first day of term, they realized it was going to be quite a challenging journey for them and they risked sitting in traffic where they were potentially exposed to greater threats,” she said.
The news comes as the couple await a verdict on their request for publicly funded security protection.
A government committee was due to review whether to provide security for the couple now that their living arrangements in the United Kingdom are more permanent.

The location of their new home has not been disclosed and questions remain over what arrangements will be in place given the protracted legal battle between Harry and the British government over the issue.
The family moved back to the United Kingdom for an “extended period” of time after six years living in Montecito, California.
Their decision to “step back” from frontline royal duties and leave the U.K. in 2020 sent shock waves around the world.
Since then, royal relations have been publicly strained, with allegations of racism and bullying made by the couple in their Netflix documentary “Harry & Meghan” and in Harry’s memoir, “Spare.”

There were new signs of strain last week, when the couple indicated they had been left “surprised” by a letter on behalf of King Charles III that reiterated they would remain private individuals and nonworking members of the royal family during their renewed stint in the U.K.
Earlier this week, Meghan shared online a series of family photos of their new life in England, showcasing her children fishing on a boat, riding bikes and taking woodland walks with their dog.
On Tuesday morning, she paid tribute to her husband on his 42nd birthday, saying that he was “simply the best.”

title: How Ukraine’s futuristic war could get ‘much worse,’ according to ex-Google CEO
summary: “The rate of innovation is faster than I’ve ever seen, and I work in tech,” Eric Schmidt told NBC News’ Richard Engel.
story: Ukraine’s battlefield “kill zones,” where leaving your bunker can mean death by Russian drone within minutes, look set to grow swiftly as the war drives breathtaking technological advancements, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has warned.

Schmidt, now CEO and executive chairman of rocket maker Relativity Space, is helping Ukraine fight a technological battle with the Kremlin that moves so quickly that weapons can lose their advantage within months.

“The rate of innovation is faster than I’ve ever seen, and I work in tech,” Schmidt told Richard Engel, NBC News’ chief foreign correspondent. Schmidt previously chaired the U.S. National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence and has advised the Pentagon.
As Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine stretches into its fifth year, Schmidt said Moscow is becoming better at developing and deploying new weapons, eroding an advantage Ukraine had relied on.

“Historically, Ukraine was this small, really smart, really fast innovator, and the Russians were, if you will, big, slow, not very capable. That’s changed,” he said in an interview for the weekly global affairs podcast “The World with Richard Engel and Yalda Hakim.”

The conflict has become a testing ground for drone warfare and thus the place for some of the technology’s latest advancements. From the Ukrainian towns now covered in anti-drone netting to the sites deep inside Russia vulnerable to attack from Kyiv, drones have become the war’s defining weapon.
President Donald Trump, who during his election campaign promised to resolve the conflict in 24 hours, has repeatedly pressured Ukraine to cede key territory and favored Moscow’s hard-line demands.
Winning would depend on how quickly either side could get its latest inventions into widespread use, Schmidt argued.
“Whoever plays the game of fastest innovation to scale will win this war,” he said.

Ukraine appears to agree with Schmidt’s assessment. The country’s new top general, Mykhailo Drapatyi, put innovation on a list of priorities he published after taking the position, saying Ukraine must learn faster than the enemy on the battlefield.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also recently noted the jet-powered Shahed drones problem, saying the Defense Ministry and the military must work on capabilities to intercept them.
Schmidt expects artificial intelligence eventually to help computers direct drone swarms, using the results of attacks to improve how they fight.
“Humans can’t run a swarm of 1,000 drones, but a computer can,” he said. “So what I think will happen is computers will develop war plans within a swarm.”
For troops on either side, the drones already in use have made leaving cover dangerous.
“The battlefield today is a no man’s land where nothing moves because there are drones and anti-drones above you,” he said.

Small “first-person view,” or FPV, drones have become the war’s bullets, hunting exposed troops, Schmidt said. Russian aircraft also drop powerful glide bombs on Ukrainian positions, threatening soldiers who remain in their shelters.

Russian troops are suffering heavy losses, too. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry estimates that 42,020 were killed or wounded in August, roughly 1,350 a day, following 42,860 in July. It described August’s toll as among the highest since the full-scale invasion began.
Britain’s military chief, Air Chief Marshal Richard Knighton, said last week that Russia’s total casualties had reached 1.5 million, including approximately 500,000 dead.
“The death rate on the Russia side is horrible. It’s just horrible, and these are human beings, too,” Schmidt said.
Russia, meanwhile, has fitted some Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones with small, inexpensive Chinese jet engines, Schmidt said, making them faster than the interceptors Ukraine uses against them.
“So how do you intercept a faster drone? Well, you have to add your own jet engine to the anti-drone,” he said.

The jet-powered drones can reach a cruising speed of over 300 miles per hour, compared with a reported 110 miles per hour of older versions, according to the Open Source Munitions Portal, a weapons-tracking project.
Eight months ago, Ukrainian teams had been successfully countering Shaheds, he said. Now they are having to find ways to stop the faster versions.
He argued that Western countries should be doing more to learn from Ukraine’s experience and help it respond.
“How could we not be capturing this knowledge in the West to defend our own countries?” he asked.

Ukraine is also competing for American weapons. In March, Zelenskyy told NBC News he feared the war with Iran could divert U.S. supplies to the Middle East, although he said scheduled deliveries to Kyiv had not been disrupted at that point.

Schmidt warned the fighting could develop into “total war,” with Ukrainians determined to resist because they fear defeat would destroy their families. “Everything in both countries is a target for everything else. That’s just horrible,” he added.
He also held out the hope that powerful computer systems might deter both sides from attacking, each unable to predict how the other would respond.
“They need Western help,” he said of Ukraine. “In particular, they need some money, and they need technological help in order to counter this set of waves coming.”
“If that help comes, I think Ukraine can hold.”

title: 10-year Treasury yield tops 5% as oil surges and diesel hits all-time high
summary: Talks between Iran and Gulf countries about the future of the Strait of Hormuz were delayed after a key Saudi pipeline was hit.
story: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield briefly topped 5% Monday for the first time since 2023 as the price of oil surged and the nationwide average cost of diesel fuel hit an all-time high.

Fears about those higher fuel prices feeding overall inflation are helping drive up yields. The Federal Reserve is widely expected to hike interest rates Wednesday for the first time since 2023. As of Monday, market odds for a hike were greater than 90%.

Longer-term bond yields, such as the 30-year Treasury bonds, rose to more than 5.37% on Monday, continuing to push to their highest levels since 2007. Consumer interest rates, such as those for mortgages, typically follow moves in bond yields.
Fuel prices shifted after Saudi Arabia shut a critical pipeline and talks about the future of the Strait of Hormuz were postponed.
The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, surged to more than $109 a barrel, while U.S. crude oil nearly hit $105.
By the end of the day, the increase had moderated. Brent closed the day up 1%, at $105.68 per barrel, and U.S. crude ended the trading session up 1.3%, at $101.39.

The East-West Pipeline, a key route for energy supplies, became even more critical because of the stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz, where vessel traffic has barely reached double digits in recent days.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Monday that he did not have an exact time frame for when the pipeline may restart but that he was in contact with his Saudi counterpart and believed it would be “very soon.”

“I might have more of a time frame tomorrow,” he told Bloomberg Television. “They’ve been very carefully assessing what the damage was, what needs to be done, and I think more clarity on that will come out very soon.”

On Friday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said the pipeline was shut down “as a precautionary measure.” It did not say when the pipeline would be operational again. The attacks came as the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen made sweeping gains that tightened their grip on Bab el Mandeb, another critical waterway.
But the pipeline could be “out of service for weeks as the damage is repaired,” The Associated Press reported later Monday, citing two regional officials.

Adding to investors’ worries, a meeting between Iran and Persian Gulf countries about Hormuz was postponed Sunday afternoon. That meeting, set for Monday, was delayed “in the interests of consensus,” Oman’s foreign minister wrote on X.
Tehran said the meeting was postponed at the request of Riyadh.
On Monday, the Saudi state-run news agency said Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met with Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command, in Jeddah.

Traffic through Hormuz remains at just a small fraction of pre-Iran war levels. On Sunday, just 14 vessels passed through the strait, and the numbers were only 12 Saturday, 11 Friday and nine Thursday, according to data from MarineTraffic.
With crude oil prices rising as a result of those disruptions, gasoline prices are, too. On Monday, the national average price of unleaded regular gas rose to $4.31 per gallon, according to AAA.
The national average price of regular gas has risen more than 45% since the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war. The price of U.S. crude oil has soared more than 50% since the war started Feb. 28.
Since the start of the year, oil prices have risen more than 80%.
On top of that, the price of diesel fuel continues to set all-time highs. The national average price of diesel rose to $6.23 per gallon Monday, AAA also reported.
Diesel, which is used in everything from trucking to boat transportation to trains, has become a particular focus for economists who say it could cause almost everything to cost more.
“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk said in a recent interview with NBC News.
“From running a farm ... [to the] cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped,” she said. When diesel prices rise, everything “gets that extra fee tacked onto it.”
Swonk predicted that the high cost of diesel will be an “inflationary problem” for months to come.
On Sunday, President Donald Trump sought to act on the issue by urging Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian energy targets.

Trump told reporters at the Irish Open in Doonbeg, Ireland, that he recently spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and asked him to stop targeting Russia’s oil refining infrastructure, particularly because of what is happening with the soaring price of diesel fuel.
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing,” Trump said. “He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.”
“Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel,” Trump continued. “Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”

ING commodities analysts said Monday: “The growing scale and intensity of Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries this year have pushed Moscow to ban diesel exports. This has only tightened global markets, following Persian Gulf disruptions.”
Russia’s ban on diesel exports is set to expire at the end of September, but “clearly, there is the potential for further extensions,” ING’s team said.
After diesel prices fell as low as $4.77 per gallon in late June, new escalations between Ukraine and Russia have driven them 30% higher.
Since the start of the year, they have soared 75%.

title: China dismisses AI slowdown calls and blasts ‘fearmongering’ from U.S. tech leaders
summary: Urgent calls for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence may cite a grave threat to humanity, but China says the warnings are instead aimed at slowing its progress as America’s rival superpower.
story: HONG KONG — China has dismissed urgent calls to slow down the development of AI, rejecting the grave warnings as a bid to hobble the progress of America’s rival superpower rather than safeguard humanity’s future.
Beijing on Monday dismissed the intervention from U.S. tech leaders as “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook.”

It’s the latest sign that competition between the two countries could outweigh mounting safety concerns, after President Donald Trump also rebuffed the warnings from industry leaders and said his focus was on beating China on artificial intelligence.
The comments followed a lengthy essay published Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk.

Amodei said that companies should deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their models given the potential risks. He also said that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world,” and called for the U.S. to restrict sales of key tech to China.
That message was not welcomed by Beijing.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve no one’s interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters at a regular news briefing Monday.

The state-run Global Times newspaper had a more blunt tone Sunday, blasting the call for an industrywide slowdown as “packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.”
AI has advanced at a breakneck speed, with models rapidly getting smarter, faster and cheaper. They have also frequently outpaced technical safeguards, fueling security fears.
Those fears have now reached a peak but also exposed just how far apart Beijing and Washington seem to be on cooperating to address them.
Amodei himself likened the situation to the Cold War arms race, telling CBS’ “‘Sunday Morning” that the two sides should work together but that he didn’t hold out much hope.
Altman similarly said on X late Sunday that “where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination.”
But that might not be compatible with Trump’s approach.

“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” the president told reporters Sunday. He criticized “very negative forces” for bringing up things “that won’t happen.”
While Trump rebuffs safety concerns, Beijing has acknowledged AI security risks.

State Security Minister Chen Yixin said Sunday that China must “accelerate the establishment of a system for preventing and controlling AI security risks.” Chen also said in the state-run China Cyberspace magazine that “we must engage extensively in international cooperation,” identifying AI as “a new track for strategic rivalry.”
The difference in approach on tackling AI progress is likely to be a central issue when Xi and Trump meet Sept. 24 in Washington.
Amodei’s essay came just a few days after U.S. agencies published an alert saying that top China AI companies have systematically copied cutting-edge AI models from American companies.
Beijing rejected this accusation that its companies had been “distilling” U.S. models.
China has also rejected any outside take on how its companies should pace development.

“They want to write the rules. I don’t think they want to follow anybody else’s,” Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a nonresident scholar at Carnegie China, told NBC News in a phone interview.
“There’s the sort of talk of cooperation, but the behavior suggests otherwise, and underlying that behavior, I think, is this deep mutual suspicion,” Chong said.

Chinese companies now offer advanced AI performance at a fraction of the cost of U.S. models, with President Xi Jinping pitching China as a pioneer of open-source models in contrast to those produced by most leading American companies.
At the BRICS summit in India on Sunday, he offered member nations help to develop open-source AI. Xi has also outlined a potential global governance framework on AI among the Global South.
How exactly could AI cause widespread danger?
Chong said the distillation clash highlighted the suspicion toward China in both the White House and Silicon Valley.

“It’s a bit like an arms race. And to get de-escalation there needs to be simultaneous neutral self-restraint and it’s difficult to see how that would come about in this kind of environment,” Chong said.
But not everyone is so pessimistic.

While a U.S.-China agreement on curbing AI progress may be a long shot, the countries could separately pursue greater regulation, said Theo Bertram, director of the London-based Social Market Foundation.
“The idea that we could see the domestic introduction of some safeguards in both countries is not impossible,” Bertram said in a phone interview.

“You do it domestically and it’s in everyone’s interest to learn and share and for there to be accountability,” he said. “Some greater accountability is one way of trying to mitigate what is inevitably going to be a growing political and public demand globally.”
